title: Ellen Halliday’s diary: Pregnancy in a polluted city
gist: A pregnant London commuter's antenatal carbon-monoxide test flagged red after a half-hour Underground ride, prompting the author to cite a new King's College London study linking early-pregnancy exposure to London traffic pollution with worse language and motor skills in babies.

insights.claim: The first study into the effects of traffic pollution on babies of mothers pregnant in London, published in 2026 by researchers at King's College London, found that exposure to pollution in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy was linked to worse language skills, with effects seen even more strongly among babies born pre-term.
insights.speaker: Ellen Halliday
insights.so_what: A newly published, London-specific research finding linking early-pregnancy urban air pollution exposure to measurable child developmental outcomes—relevant to public health policy debates on London air quality (e.g. ULEZ) and to any assessment of urban pollution's long-term societal costs.

insights.claim: The King's College London study found that motor skills in babies were also worse when mothers were exposed to traffic pollution in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, while exposure later in pregnancy did not show the same association, and it remains unknown whether affected children catch up later in life.
insights.speaker: Ellen Halliday
insights.so_what: Narrows the pollution-exposure risk window to the first trimester specifically, a more precise and actionable finding for public health guidance than a general 'pollution is bad for pregnancy' claim.
insights.locator: Exposure in later pregnancy didn’t have the same association

insights.claim: The author's own antenatal carbon-monoxide breath test showed a 'danger' red reading after a half-hour ride on the London Underground's Victoria line, despite her never having smoked—illustrating that ordinary London commuting can trigger the same clinical pollution marker used to flag smokers.
insights.speaker: Ellen Halliday
insights.so_what: A vivid first-person data point suggesting standard antenatal carbon-monoxide screening may be poorly calibrated to distinguish smoking from ordinary urban transit exposure, with potential implications for how NHS antenatal protocols interpret readings for non-smoking commuters.

insights.claim: The author observes that London apartment blocks and brick building materials retain and radiate heat during summer heatwaves, meaning even a shaded, ground-floor flat becomes uncomfortably hot after several consecutive heatwave days, with London Underground carriages reaching around 35 degrees Celsius during her commute.
insights.speaker: Ellen Halliday
insights.so_what: A concrete, specific illustration (35°C tube carriages) of how London's building stock and transit infrastructure amplify urban heat-island effects during heatwaves, relevant to discussions of UK infrastructure adaptation needs as heatwaves become more frequent.
